utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest during the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for your interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher's assistance, please to return to the witness where we left off on Friday with Exhibit P239.11?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We were talking about that a bit, sir, and I think we got so far as you said that in fact, if I understand you correctly, these reports were not in fact regularly kept, for whatever reason, due to lack of perhaps resources or the effort involved or what have you, but did I understand you correctly on Friday that the type of regular reporting that was contemplated in this document, from Mr. Stojic, on the 6th of February, 1993, that that process was never, according to you, really fully put into place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I kindly ask you to assist me when a question is put in this way? Because I don't really know how to answer such a question. The Prosecutor is trying to ask me as the old prophet Propertius [phoen],"ibis, redibis, non, morieris in bello," "you shall go, you shall return, you shall never perish in the war." Depending on where the comma is I have to tell what the question is. I really don't understand the Prosecutor because in one allegation, one allegation contains several questions and several wrong allegations, and then he says; is that correct? Is that the normal way the Court functions? And finally, I would like to know what document, what exhibit, are we talking about? Because I have a number of exhibits in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe Mr. Scott, you could help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And try to ask a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I referred a few movements ago and perhaps there was some confusion with the documents, I specifically referred your attention to P239.11, which I believe is probably the first or second document in the bundle that I think I see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which document you're referring to, before they put it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have it now, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is 515095.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what number you're referring to, sir, I'm referring to a document that has exhibit number on the first page, P239.11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. Thank you for giving me the floor. I would like to assist the Honourable Court. Our Croatian copies do not contain any numbers but the Prosecution numbers in the right, top corner. So this is 01515095. This is the number that the witness has just read to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the witness has already found that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir my question to you, forgive me if it was too complicated. I thought it was rather straightforward. Did you tell us on Friday, that despite Mr. Stojic's orders of the 6th of February, 1993, that a regular reporting system on these matters was not in fact implemented?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not what I said. Can I please clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order refers to a department which, for a certain period of time, engaged in the research of crimes committed over the civilian population by primarily but also soldiers, those who were detained, and then killed. I believe that this dates to 6th of -- I don't know which month because I can't see very well. This is not the 6th of February. I believe this was either 6th of July or 6 August. So this is a document that originated after an event which took place in the already mentioned Doljani, when the Muslim forces detained 27 or 37 soldiers, among whom there were also ten civilians, and they were all killed. Then we asked for a post mortem to take place of all the civilians who had been killed after being tortured it. We wanted to have the confirmation that that they had indeed been tortured. I already said that this department -- that the person in charge of that department was Dr. Brncic, and that something indeed was being done with that regard but I never did -- never did she publish her work on that topic, which doesn't mean that no crimes involving the civilians and the soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council took place. What I said that wasn't done was that she did not write a book on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, none of those were my questions. I know you're anxious to tell this Chamber about war crimes you believe were committed against the Croats and you have my sympathy in that regard but that was not the question I put to you, sir. Was this information in fact, as ordered in the order of in Stojic, was that information in fact systematically collected by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is not appropriate it to allow the Prosecution to give us their presumptions, why the witness is here. What is clear is that the witness is here to answer the questions put to him. The Prosecution should not be allowed the comments in the way he has just put them, and this is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the question put by the Prosecution is very simple. The question is a regular reporting system on those matters was not in fact implemented. The witness has the choice to answer this question, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not object to the question. I do not object to the question. I object to the Prosecutor's comments. I don't know whether you have that in the transcript. I believe you do have it. The Prosecutor proposed his comments and the comment was, "You are here to tell us all about the Croatian victims." This was not the question. I object to the comments which I deem inappropriate. I heard these comments loud and clear, and I never objected to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution said that he has "his sympathy in this regard. That was not the question I put to you." I don't think he is improper in this regard. Witness, you may answer the question put by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Honours. This order refers to the units of the Croatian Defence Council in respect of their respective areas of responsibility. The order meant that if a body was found and that if there was suspicion that a crime had been committed involving either a civilian or a soldier, a post mortem should be carried out. I repeat, it doesn't say that here but I know this. This order was issued in order to help this particular person to collect a certain number of data. She is, I believe, a member of the association for victims or human rights centres, with a view for her to publishing a book, and what I said and I repeat, she never published that book. Last time when I said that nothing was done, I didn't mean that post mortems were not done. If you're asking me whether post mortems were done, then I can answer that but the way the Prosecutor is asking me, I cannot answer simply yes or no, because my answer would not be correct. It cannot be either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you know, was this order, to your knowledge, since you were the director of the health care sector or health services of the HVO, was this only to collect war crime information concerning Croat victims or was it also to collect information about Muslim civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said, this order was issued after an event that had taken place in Doljani village. So that is when the need arose for such an order to be issued. I know that this lady doctor wanted to author a book about Croatian civilian victims of crimes. This does not mean that this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't want to spend our time talking about this book. It's about the fourth answer we've now had about this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, sir: Did the HVO ever collect information, make a systematic effort to collect information about the killing of Muslim civilians and collect that information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I don't know. This is not within my scope of authority, nor I personally was involved in that. So I don't know. I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So what you're telling the Chamber, sir, is that as the most senior medical officer in the HVO, you have no knowledge of any systematic effort by the HVO to collect -- to collect information on Muslim civilian war crime victims?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really sometimes wonder about what you're saying. You're talking about somebody who was in charge of health care, whose task was to organise that health care, for whom? For everybody and everywhere. This is what we can talk about, and I can provide you with any possible answer and I can, because I know the answers. Now you're asking me things that have nothing whatsoever to do with me and you're asking me to say either yes or no, but this was beyond my authority and I was not involved in that, in the main medical headquarters, there was a department which was in charge of the fallen members of the HVO. It could, of course, not look after the fallen members of the Army of BH, because the opposition side never sent us any information about their fallen soldiers. At that time, we were the ones who collected such data because nobody before us endeavoured to collect them. And we wanted to do that in order to monitor or to be able to provide people with data, to monitor where somebody was wounded, when -- where somebody was treated. So in answer to your question, whether somebody systematically collected data on the Croatian victims besides us, I really don't know, and I particularly don't know whether anybody was in charge of collecting data on the fallen Muslim soldiers or civilians. That I really don't know. That was not my job. That was not what I was authorised to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P601.2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I go back to that previous question? Because something has just occurred to me with regard to it my previous comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe you have answered this question already but if you have something to add, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this order that I have just seen, and that I never saw before, I know where this order came from, and since I was Dr. Brncic's superior, I asked the minister to send that order to the field, and I can see here that what it says in this order, that in case a crime had been committed involving civilians, that people should be referred to our pathology department. What I would like to say here is that we did not have a pathology, and throughout the war, we did not have a single pathologist in Mostar. Unfortunately the clinical hospital in Mostar to this very day does not have a pathologist. These individual cases, when they were found, as many as were found, I know they referred to the pathology department of the clinical hospital in Split and this I claim with certainty. And that is the end of my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To follow up on that, sir, this is Split in the Republic of Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am referring to the city that I already mentioned on my -- on the first day when I started giving my testimony. Split was an institution which looked after all the Croats, Muslims and Serbs which we couldn't treat. So this is the city, i.e. the clinics that admitted a number of thousands of people from Bosnia and Herzegovina and their pathology department provided the service that is they could provide when needed. So when a body was referred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to 601.2, if you look at that for a moment, sir, and can you tell the Chamber, are you familiar with that kind of -- type of report, not only this particular document but with this type of report, reporting wounded and dead soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you will allow me to take a look at this document, because there are several pages in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness starts giving the answer, I would kindly ask my learned friend to tell us the source of this document because the date is 16 September, and the reports were sent on the 17th September, 20 September, and the document was issued on the 16th of September. How is that possible? The report was issued on the 16th of September and the data referred to the 17th and 20th of September. Maybe there is some magic involved here and maybe somebody knows in advance who is going to be killed and where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First of all the source of the document that's indicated on the B/C/S original is the Zagreb archive. You can clearly see the marking of the stamp in the upper right-hand corner of the first page of the original document. As for the dates, Mr. President, I cannot answer that. This document purports to have been created by there witness. It's over his signature, bearing a stamp. So perhaps the witness can tell us it may have been a mistake. It maybe any number of things but it's not for me to say and I object to counsel getting up and going into this before the witness is ever given a chance. This is a recurring problem we have been through this week after week after week. The defence gets up before the witness has a chance to answer and makes objections or talks about the document. We object to that procedure. And we will continue to object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, if you have some objections, you may save it until the witness answers the question. We understand that this document was signed by the witness. Maybe he could shed some light on this very issue. But do not -- but do not give any hint to this witness before he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not giving instructions to my witness. What I'm asking from this Honourable Court is to disallow the abuse of the cross-examination. The witness has to be informed about the data from the document in a proper way. The witness must not be cheated and the document has not been signed by the witness, and why do we always create this confusion? This document was not signed by the witness. We know only too well what is a person's signature and what is somebody's name typed. I'm just trying to object to the abuse, to the cross-examination being abused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I don't think it's a proper way for you to make this kind of objections at this time. There should be some rules for this. If the witness denied this document, he has the full right to say it, to explain it, to this Tribunal. There is no need for you to tell the witness that he does not sign this document, there is some strange dates in this document, and et cetera. If you have objections after we hear the witness, you also have the full right to object. But do not give any hint to this witness before he answers the question. Yes, witness, you may answer this question. Have you read this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is very difficult to read such a long document, but, yes, I'm now acquainted with the document and that is enough. I would like to ask the Honourable Court that not to be defended by either the Prosecutor or the Defence counsel because I don't need that. I just need your protection and when I say that, I mean for you to allow me to talk. There is no question that I cannot answer here, and there is no question that I will not try to answer. I will never say, "I don't know." I will always answer. The document that I have in my hand, I can't recall, because we had a number, hundreds, of papers, every day. So this could be one of them. The proof that this paper most probably originates from the Defence department is my signature, not my signature, but my facsimile, so if this document is not forged, I don't know whether it is or not, but if it is not a forgery, then it can only originate from the institution where I worked. So this is the confirmation of the thesis that I mentioned a little while ago, and confirms the existence of that department, that look after the dead and the wounded. We had women working at the computer and entering data. That means that I did not have to sit beside them. They received information from the field, about those who were either killed or wounded, and they inputted the data into the computer. What I find very strange about this document is the following: For which purpose was this paper used? We never had any printouts that were their own purpose. Whenever we had to print such a document, it would be to send it to somebody. This paper doesn't give the addressee's name or address. If I were to send it to somebody, then I would have certainly signed it personally. I believe that without my signature, that my name was on the -- on this paper is possible because my name was in the computer, in the computer programme. So whatever was inputted into the computer my name would be put on the bottom of that document. So that is not disputable. What is disputable about this document is that there is no addressee. I recognise some brigades, I recognise some units, and I can tell that this document mentions only the dead and the wounded soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council. Another thing that surprises me, can be found on the last page, on which it says, "Wounded civilians or killed civilians." I don't know who these civilians are, whether they were wounded in Mostar or elsewhere, and then brought to our hospital. I don't know. And I also don't know the breakdown of these people, who they belonged to. In one place here, I can see on page -- just a moment, please -- on page 5 of this document, it says, killed soldiers on 16 September, 1993. 3rd Brigade. So this is a report which speaks about that. I expect further questions and I -- because I don't know what the question is. We did have a database containing the names of the killed and wounded members of the HVO. Whether anybody else was inputted into that data base, I don't know. I couldn't control that. That was not my task. We had women who were in charge of that, who were experts, working on computers, and -- but I do believe that this paper does originate from the health department. It does not give the addressee's name and I don't know why it was printed. Why would the women print the document if it wasn't to be sent to anybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know how this information was collected, sir, about the number of soldiers wounded or killed. Looking at the first page of Exhibit P601.2 it lists in the first section for 16th of September, 1993, ten persons, starting with one name Slaven Martinovic. Can you tell the Chamber, please, I'm only using this particular document as an example of one which you can tell us could have been one of many of a similar type of report that was prepared, and my question to you is: How would that information be collected?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for a clear and fair question. That is a question in which I do not see that you are trying to make me say something that was not correct. And that could possibly be against somebody. And that does not exist. So my congratulations. The information that we collected, all information that reached us in relation to this point that we are discussing now, came from doctors on the ground, and I will now try, Your Honours, to explain briefly one thing, so that it doesn't happen again that the Prosecutor asks me how regularly did they come, how frequently, who did you send reports to. So let me clarify that. So, we had physicians across Bosnia, in Posavina, Zepce with which we had no communication whatsoever, in Novo Selo [phoen] with whom we had no communication whatsoever and let me not enumerate further. I do into the want to wear you down. But we had the packet link and at times it worked, at times it didn't. I consider that in the health care, we maintained better communication with the ground than others, because we are, if nothing else, doctors. We are more educated. So that we did not introduce all the information that we received from different sides. Needless to say, at that time, neither I nor anyone else could check on every single individual. So what we received from physicians on the ground, we put in. It wasn't I who did that. I repeat. It was those who were responsible for them. What we didn't, we didn't. And that now was used exclusively as a data base, as a data base so that we could use it in case, for instance, when somebody came to us and started looking for his kin, be it wounded or killed, and if they come and give their name, then they type this name, feed it into the computer and then this girl sitting at the computer tells us, yes, this or that happened on that, on such and such date. That was the purpose of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, in reference to the first section on the first page of P601.2, when we see on the first list, number 6, we can conclude, then, that this person, this soldier, was a member of the Convicts Battalion, who was a casualty on the 16th of September, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if that is correct, Your Honours, because nobody checked this information. I have already said that. This means, when we received information from the ground, that is our workers, they would type it in as they had received it, whether this is correct or not, I guarantee that nobody can say, nobody can tell that. And I repeat, I do not understand the purpose of this document, who are we sending it to? And I have to observe another thing, Mr. Krsnik was right, that is I do not understand how could the document be signed on the 16th and then we have woundings on the 17th, on the 19th, on the 20th, and so on. So let me come back to the question. Let me be specific. I do not know, just as I do not know the largest number of these people, and I cannot know them and I cannot know whether this man was indeed a member of the Convicts Battalion or not, and who and where, who he belonged to or whether he was wounded at all. Because nobody checked that, and that was not our priority, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, would you please try to give us concise answers? If the Prosecutor needs more information, he will ask you some questions. I think the answer could only be put as "I don't know." That's a very simple answer. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, was it not true, is it not true, that the HVO, as any other military organisation, was interested in collecting information about its casualties, wounded, dead, what have you? That's information that the army would want to know, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO is not military formation, structure. It was both civilian and military. Number 1. Number 2, I repeat, this information that we collected had to do where -- were intended only to follow up on the wounded and I was not interested in any other aspect, nor did anyone ask me or use it to make, I don't know, some estimates of the combat preparedness of the army or anything, but simply so that we could have some files about the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can be answered yes or no. Was the HVO as a military organisation, the military side of the HVO, and you know quell what I'm talking about, was that organisation interested in collecting and recording information about its casualties? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to know that. I do not know about the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as the senior medical officer in the HVO military organisation, sir, isn't it true that the collection and recording of that information fell, if not entirely, largely to the section or unit, what have you, the department, under your control?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The filing and collection was my last priority during the war. My first question was the organisation of health care and that is my -- that is my answer. That is my answer. Listen to me. I will really ask to be protected. My interest was to treat people and to look after that, at the same time, if it was to monitor the wounded and killed in that direction, then I did it but for no other reason. So that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, please cool down at this moment. Understand during the cross-examinations, both parties are hostile to each other. The Chamber will judge by ourselves. So if there is an answer -- if there is a question, you just answer that question and don't get excited. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the collection of that information, this -- these type of documents, such as 601.2, would not necessarily have to be addressed to anyone, would they? They would simply be a collection and a record of the information collected, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is almost correct. That is correct. It was gathered so that one could be able to take stock of the situation if doctors came or something. I do not remember if we ever notified anyone about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While I understand that you can not vouch for the accuracy of any particular entry in these records, you and your department were certainly interested and wanted accurate information, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, God himself cannot answer that question. Commanders, unit commanders, Your Honours, knew which of their men had been wounded or killed, so I didn't have to tell them that. This was kept exclusively in this central part so that we could have information. Therefore I really don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, Mr. Scott, can I get this cross-examination back on track? Perhaps it would be easier, Dr. Bagaric, if you were to explain to us and it would help us if you would tell us what was the protocol which you ordained in our hospital for the collection of data in relation to war victims? How did you direct your staff to enter the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is a good question, and I think that at long last, I see a way out, but I have to clear it up. The -- I apologise but there is no other way. This information, which this gentleman has brought here, this is not the hospital information. This is not the information of a particular unit. This is the information collected at our staff, and the staff was an institution which incorporated all hospitals and all units. So we fed information into the computer on the basis of reports from the field, from the hospitals, that is, from brigades, from places more removed or less removed. Needless to say, every unit also kept its records, so did every hospital, and I do not doubt that but I wasn't the director of a hospital. I really cannot speak about any hospital. But I believe that that was an institution which did its work, proper work, and I do believe they do have protocols, when persons were admitted, whether they were wounded, how they were wounded when they were discharged. So this is my answer and I believe you understand me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could clear something up for me because I understood that you were the director of the hospital and therefore that you might actually prepare -- but you were the director of the whole service. I see. So did these -- this information come into your computer from a number of hospitals and treatment centres, not necessarily from the Mostar war hospital? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And did you want that information as accurate as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely, quite so. I was the commander of the health care department of the Croat Defence Council so I was above any hospital and whatever hospital. The fact that for a while, I was in the area of the Mostar hospital with my office, that has nothing to do with the Mostar hospital. So what we are talking about now, it was information we received from the ground. What information, how much of the information, how accurate, how complete it is, I really cannot say but what I know certainly especially when it comes to distant parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that that information was complete because I do not believe that they were from every Bosnian back water we received information about the wounded and killed. Whatever information we received we fed into the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance, please, to hand you Defence Exhibit D1/381, 371, and 379? Let me repeat that in order, 371, 379 and 381.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for the way I reacted a moment ago. I really do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention in order -- if you'll first direct your attention to D1/371, and I'll direct your particular attention and the courtroom's attention to the last page, and that is of the Croatian language version of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am -- I can follow both the Croatian and the English version. Please, I see that not every word is properly conveyed. I know that our interpreters are in serious trouble because the witness is very fast but I assure you that 30 per cent of what the meaning of what the witness said has not been included correctly. Of course it is nobody's fault except that the witness is very fast. So could you please warn him to slow down? To slow down his speed? And that is perhaps what gives rise to misunderstanding because the witness is saying one thing and you are receiving a different thing through interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, that's a very serious allegation you said about 30 per cent of what the witness said is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, not in that sense that it is not correct but I mean the meaning, because I hear exactly what the witness is saying because I can follow him in Croatian and you are meeting for the first time with this, the way it was interpreted there can be some misunderstanding between your questions and the reactions with regard to what the witness is saying, that's what I said, not that the transcript has lost what was said, no, not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you see the difficulty in this it Tribunal. Whatever you said has to be translated into two other languages. So when you are answering a question, please make stops after every sentence and please say it slowly so that we could follow you. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exhibit D1/371, the last page, as I look at this document, sir, it has neither a stamp nor a signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there is no stamp nor signature to this document but it is even more true that I wrote this paper and sent it and signed it. This is just a computer copy. So a moment ago, this paper that had no -- that did not have my signature, I said that as likely as not it had been produced by us, but about this text, Your Honours, I know certainly, because I wrote that word for word, sentence for sentence and this was sent to international organisations which are indicated here as addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, why is it that it doesn't have your signature and a stamp on it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature and my stamp are completely needless here because I left behind works. I left also the signature and the stamp. I can of course try and find the document that I signed at the time. That is, I thought that the deeds were more important. When I wanted to show this and what I have done. Whether some of this has a signature and a stamp, if that is really -- if this document is brought into question, because it lacks a signature and a stamp, then I assure you, Your Honours, I undertake to find this document with a signature and a stamp. And this document can also be found in the UN and the UNHCR, and the ICRC. Ivan Bagaric would not be sitting here telling lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did I understand you a moment ago to say that the original letter that was sent out would be signed and stamped but a computer generated copy or a file copy maintained in your office would not be signed and stamped?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. So a document that I sent was signed, no doubt, and had its stamp. But this document, this document is not possible. I do not understand this technology, when -- how can I sign it while the document is still in the computer. So that's it. It has to be printed first. And this is just one copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, wouldn't you agree that any number of documents could fall in that same category, work copies, file copies, non-originals, electronic copies could be completely authentic and completely accurate that would not bear a signature or a stamp?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is my document, which I sent to these organisations, and which I signed. It means nothing that it is not signed here. I can find the document which has been signed. And that same document can be found with the international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, would you look, please, as Exhibit D1/379? I'll direct your attention -- I'm not going to ask you about the contents of the document, sir, I'm just going to ask you to look at the last page again. It purports to be prepared by someone, forgive me if I say it wrong, Brncic. Would you agree with plea, sir, that there is no signature on that document, or stamp, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this document, the same explanation that I can give applies to this document as to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... first answer my question and if somebody wants an explanation, we can talk to you about that, it does not bear a sample or signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I remember often your warnings, addressed to me when I conducted cross-examination and you told me very wisely too, if there is a conflict or for instance, a situation which is not improper situation between a counsel and a witness, that you will always blame the counsel, because he is a professional. So we have to take care how we question witnesses. The witness, as I can see, is very garrulous person, a very reputable person and you can see that I also conducted my examination with difficulty. Namely this witness is simply answering in a manner which do not fit into the rules, if I may put it that way. And if he thinks that something needs to be explained, then will this Honourable Court allow him for such -- to it allow him such explanations of course briefly because our time is precious? Will you please warn the Prosecutor to conduct the cross-examination just as you warned me, and of course, it was because of my temperament, of which I'm aware, and you always respected it and I appreciate it. That the Prosecutor will be accountable, will be responsible, if there is a conflict, not the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe in this instance, the Prosecutor asked a very simple question which everybody knows by looking at this document. That is there is no signature on that document or stamp, correct? All the witness should answer is yes or no. If he needs some explanations, if we are interested in the explanations, we will allow the witness to give an explanation, but here, we only want to hear his -- are there any signatures and stamps? That's a very, very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. You're absolutely right. But this is not the problem. The problem is the fact that the witness wants to explain, the Prosecution does not allow the witness to explain, and the witness does not accept the way the cross-examination is conducted. Not in the way the Prosecution wants to do it. I just wanted to ask you to it allow him that, to give him that concession, in order to avoid conflicts. I'm not objecting to any of the questions. I'm not objecting to the way the cross-examination is conducted. And the witness starts, the situation is like with the previous document, and the Prosecution interrupts him very -- and it is not disputable that there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I answer in the way I was asked to answer by the Prosecution? I will, from now on, answer in that way, no matter what that will mean. Although I don't believe that this is a fair way to examine me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, if the Prosecution asks you a question, first you have to answer that question. Secondly, if you need some explanations, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, everybody in this courtroom, everybody in this world, can see that there is neither signature nor stamp. I can't see any of them either. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Try to do it in a concise way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wife also tells me all the time that I am a man of too many words. This document -- I didn't show you to demonstrate that there is no signature. Everybody can see that. But I can tell the Honourable Court this document is authentic. It was signed, and it can be corroborated by the person who signed it. I know what this document is all about. This is another copy from the document, and only the original is signed. You don't sign all the five copies. In this case, the original was sent to the foreign press bureau. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was exactly what my inquiry was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was my inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that the Muslim side or the ABiH on a number of occasions also provided medical treatment or health care for Bosnian Croat soldiers and civilians, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is. I believe it is. However, I don't have any specific information from the BH Army doctors. I did not have any offers during the conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina for cooperation. There were no such offers. But I do believe that they also treated Croatians. And I even know that they did so in some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, so not only do you assume that but in fact you know that to be the case, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So sir, you and I can agree on this, I hope. Both sides in connection with the Croat-Muslim conflict, both sides on occasion showed thankfully so, acts of kindness to the victims on the other side, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct, Your Honours. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you need to explain that? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't think I should, then I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher please assist you with showing you Exhibit P171.1? I'm sorry, I think that the problem is, Mr. President, my apology, as of Friday the translation hadn't come in, I think now there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, about this document, is, please, you were already in your position or strike that. Were you in your position as the head of the health or medical service for the HVO at or about the time that Minister of Defence Stojic issued this order establishing the HVO detention facility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I need a translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. I assumed you had it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need a translation in Croatian. This is English. I cannot comment upon this before I see the Croatian translation. It is as if you told me that it is in the library somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the usher should have headphones. Otherwise, he can't hear that the document is in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the date of this document is 3rd of September, 1992, and the question, whether -- if it is the question, whether I was the head of the medical headquarters at the time, the answer is yes, on the 3rd of September, I was chief of the medical headquarters and that is the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with the establishment of the Heliodrom detention facility, as the senior HVO medical officer, were you tasked or ordered or directed to set up some method of providing health care at this facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, could we wait after the witness answers the question? Or are you talking about a procedural matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Procedural matter, Your Honours. I am glad that we are now moving on to the continental law. I'm going to make a note of all my objections and then, when the Prosecution is over, I will just give you the list of all the objections that I have noticed. I believe that within the Anglo-Saxon law, I have to object in advance, then I have to object in advance. Especially if I see that a document is being presented, which can not serve as the base for the cross-examination. If we are going to adhere to the continental law, then I am going to make a list of all the objections and then I will dictate them at the end of the Prosecution. The Prosecutor insists on the detention centre. It says very clearly here, "the central military prison." I apologise for taking more time and this is what I insist on, this is a procedural matter. Can I please ask our learned friend to use the terminology that is in the original document, central military prison is a very, very different from the detention centre. At least in the Croatian. I don't know about the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, really, you have to trust the bench here to deal with the procedure. I don't believe you do. We notice things up here, and we take note of things. And your witness, Dr. Bagaric, is a highly intelligent man. He would be the first to notice any misrepresentation included in a question. So really, we are interested in letting this poor witness go home. He's been here a long time. And let's try and get the flow moving and -- the witness can answer questions, I think, quite adequately. He doesn't need anyone's help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're absolutely right. Maybe I have lost trust in -- confidence in my colleague. I apologise both to him and to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, allow me, Your Honour, to thank you for saying that I'm intelligent. I've started doubting it myself. And thank you for looking after my well being. That is something I also appreciate. [In English] Excuse me, what was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no pending question to you, sir. The question that was asked first of all was, were you in your position at this time? Which you answered yes. Then before I think Mr. Krsnik objected, I had started to ask you the question: Were you tasked in connection with the creation of this central military prison, as the document clearly says, and I certainly wouldn't have tried to deceive anyone in the courtroom by my paraphrase when the document is in front of everybody, were you tasked to set some sort of medical provision system in that prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date here is the 3rd of September. I know nothing of this document, and I don't find it binding in any respect. Two days ago, I told you that I visited that prison on the first possible occasion, when I first learned about that prison, and that was earlier than this date, and that in that prison, I did set up a medical centre, medical service, which provided for the health care of the detainees. It was not on anybody's orders. Nor did anybody prevent me from doing it. As soon as I had the opportunity to do it, as soon as my colleagues had the opportunity to do it, me and my colleagues, we did it. And that, I already told you, and all of that happened prior to the date on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer to my question, sir, is no, when the prison was established on the 3rd of September, 1992, no one approached you at that time, according to you, and asked you to set up any mechanism for providing health care?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I made a mistake with regard to the year. What I see here is 1993 -- 1992, and I was talking about 1993. I don't know anything about this document which was made in 1992. I don't know anything about its authenticity, nothing about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I didn't ask you anything about the document, sir. When the prison was established, in 3 -- on the 3rd of September, 1992 and I'll just ask one last time and then I'll go on, did anyone in the HVO hierarchy, such as the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic, approach you as the senior medical officer in the HVO about making any provision for providing health care in that prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to be able to say either yes or no. And please allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the 3rd September, 1992. That was the time when there was no Croatian-Muslim conflict. That was the time when Mostar was being shelled every day, and Mostar, at the time, was defended jointly by Croats and Muslims. Therefore, I don't have any idea about the establishment of this military prison. I don't know what it could have served. I don't know that at the time something was happening. I could not intervene because nothing was going on, as far as I was concerned. This is the first time I hear about this. That's for one. And secondly, it is not necessary to have a medical service in a prison. If the detainees require medical care, then they are brought to a hospital. But subsequently, we did set up a medical centre due to extraordinary circumstances. There was a number, a huge number, of detainees there, so nobody had to order me anything. I did that have my own free judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's time for the break. If I could just ask one question on this before we break I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago you said that when you did visit the Heliodrom, you took these steps. We can go back in the transcript if necessary where you gave that answer. Can you please give the Chamber the date, the approximate date, when you -- the first and as you told us on Friday, the only time that you were personally at the Heliodrom? When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was on my return from Canada. This was probably in mid-July. I say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness just say the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will break now. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik? Do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. I have a bad feeling about a misunderstanding that I caused. I believe that I have been misunderstood. I would like to apologise to our interpreters. A little while ago, when I mentioned 30 per cent, I did not mean -- I did not say that the interpreters misinterpreted something or interpreted wrongly what the witness is saying. Whatever the witness is saying is interpreted absolutely correctly. When I said 30 per cent, I meant that the witness loses 30 per cent. I can follow him in the Croatian. But when he wants to say something, 30 per cent of what he wants to say is lost in the English translation. I did not mean by saying what I said that the interpreters were wrong and I believe that I have been misunderstood. I believe that I was wrong. That's why I feel bad. And that's why I would like to apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But still, I could not understand what you are saying, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's an example. Maybe I am -- I did not express myself well. What I'm saying is that I can follow the witness, and I can follow precisely what he is saying. And he wants to say. But when he speaks fast, and when he can not communicate his message as well as he would want to, then the interpreters obviously cannot convey that meaning. So I blame it on the witness, not on the interpreters. That is why I said that 30 per cent of what he wants to say in his answer we lose because he is too fast. That's what I meant when I said what I said. I did not for a moment want to blame the interpreters for interpreting something wrongly. That's why I feel bad. And therefore I wanted to apologise, because I value their job, I appreciate their job very much. Especially when witnesses speak fast. When I speak fast, I'm sure it is very difficult for them to follow what we say and that is why, for that bad feeling, I wanted to apologise, because I did not mean to in any case -- in any way blame them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please? Mr. Scott, I have to say that you have to finish your cross-examination in one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I will do my very best. I can assure the Chamber it may not be apparent and some may think as I heard some suggestion that I was prolonging it. I can assure the Chamber that I have taken steps at every break to repeatedly cut my material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the late summer of 1993 and continuing into the fall and the end of 1993, it was widely known, was it not, that conditions in the HVO detention camps, including the Heliodrom, Dretelj, Gabela and Ljubuski, the conditions there were all far below those required by international and medical norms, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the health care standards, the conditions in these prisons or centres were at the highest possible level which we could provide at that moment. Obviously, whatever you may do under such circumstances leaves a lot of room for improvement. But from the point of view of health care, we did everything possible -- I would say that all that was in compliance with humanitarian laws and conventions, and I would also like to say that unfortunately, in comparison to some other centres of this type, we were really well organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance in putting before you Exhibit P566.4?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I did not want to object to the document. I just want to say that we do not have the Croatian original. We haven't received it. And if my learned friend has it now, can we please have it from him? For this document, we do not have the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We don't have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think we have that yet. Just apparently as Mr. Krsnik has reminded the Chamber many times, sometimes we don't get the translations as quickly as we would like but there is only one sentence, there is only one sentence which I will read and ask the interpreters to assist, please when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the situation here different. We need to have the original, which then needs to be translated. So the original has to be given to the other side. When I have a Croatian original, I give you the Croatian original, and I give you the English translation. You cannot have the translation without the original, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the original, Your Honour. It's an English-language document. 566.4. It's not a translation. It's an English-original document. Mr. Krsnik is saying we must have the original because the original is in Croatian. It's an English document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. But you promised us that you will furnish the translation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall being visited by representatives of human rights watch, Ms. Ivana Nizic and Zeljka Markic? I'm looking at the entry Friday for August 20, 1993. On that date, on approximately the 20th of August, 1993, let me ask for the interpreters to assist me, I'm going to read one or two sentences, if you could assist me, at the end of that paragraph for August 20, quote, "We asked permission to visit the Dretelj and Gabela prisons. We asked Dr. Ivan Bagaric of the HZ HB Minister of Health to intervene with the Capljina and HZ HB authorities to visit the camps and were denied. Bagaric conceded that conditions were not satisfactory in these camps." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document calls for an explanation. I apologise. I cannot answer by simply saying yes or no. I want to explain. This is in English. And I do not have anything against providing a comment upon it. I do wish to comment upon this document. These ladies, Ivana Nizic and Zeljka Markic did not visit us. We invited them. That's number 1. Number 2, they talked to Ivan Bagaric, Health Minister. Ivan Bagaric was never Health Minister. Number 3, they did not talk only with me. They talked to a number of other doctors, amongst whom there may have also been the Health Minister, whose first name is also Ivan but his last name is different. At this moment, I cannot remember any particular sentence, because their visit lasted several days. I remember, amongst other things, that they also visited me in my office, but they also visited a number of other people's offices. It says here that the access was denied. I don't know who denied it, because I'm not that fluent in English, and in the last part of the sentence, it says, Minister of Health to intervene in -- intervene and then that this was denied. Was it I who denied it or was it somebody else who denied that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what was about the conditions in Dretelj and Gabela that were "not satisfactory"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for Ivan Bagaric, physician, and an active member in the Croat Defence Council, the very fact that these, I don't know, these investigative prisons happened, that very fact makes it unsatisfactory. It is simply had to happen. If somebody was incarcerated, that for me was and is something necessitating additional effort. So I do not know what Mrs. Zeljka Markic and that other lady, that I commented something and I just don't remember it. But what I know 100 per cent, we can call them to testify here, that they were very happy after this visit with us, and after they gained insight into the condition of their wards, whether they visited everybody, I do not know. But I know they went to Heliodrom with our doctors. So my answer, Mr. Prosecutor, is I do not remember what is it that I was not satisfied with at the time. However, I do accept that it is quite possible that in -- as I talked it with them, I possibly said that or perhaps somebody else said that, because it says here, Ivan Bagaric, Minister of Health Care. So perhaps they heard it from somebody else. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to argue with you, we don't have time. Minister of Health here is in quotation marks. Can't you understand that to me that may or may not be an exact title? They were referring to you, Dr. Ivan Bagaric, the senior HVO medical officer, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not, no. It is not. Because Minister of Health Care is a completely different individual. So Mrs. Nizic did speak with me. That is true. But not me only. She also met with the Minister of Health Care, and with five other physicians who worked in the HVO medical corps. So at this moment, I cannot say this is I. Yes, I am Ivan Bagaric, but I'm not the Minister for Health Care and I do not remember this comment that I made even though I do not want to affirm that I did not comment it in this way. It is possible that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, as Exhibit 612.2? Sir, just let me say to save time, I'm not suggesting for a moment that your name appears on here or you signed it or didn't sign it or anything, that's not my question so you need not tell me that. Would you look, though, at the content of this information, points 1 through 8, the question I'm going to put to you is this: Isn't it true, sir, that even as late as the end of September, 1993, the medical care in the camps was still inadequate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the second part of the document? Because I have only one part of the document. I only have the first part of the document. I don't have the latter part. And there is still something missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've given you the entire document that I have, sir, which bears the seal at the bottom of the page, and I've given you everything I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not the complete document because I remember this document. There is a document which came from the medical corps headquarters. And this is an important document. And there is the second part which is missing and it is signed and I can tell you who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by -- it was signed by my physicians, whose superior I was, whom I had sent to go and supervise the situation. So it is that part of the medical team that I spoke about last time, on the one but last, that we had set up outside the centre one of the medical points so as to organise, carry out and so on and so forth, another thing I take great pride in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say you know who it is. Please give us the name.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you are forcing me to tell you that I won't give you the names now. If I said, why do you interrupt me? I will say everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm doing the best to follow the Chamber's guidance to finish the examination in one hour, so if the answers could please be limited and responsive it will assist me in trying to meet the Chamber's guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, the Prosecutor asked you the question, what is the name of that physician? If you need to protect that person, we would go into the private session for that. But you are obliged to answer the questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand what you're saying, and I suggest that the Prosecutor should not make haste and not examine me for one hour but as long as it takes because I'm not in a hurry today. Today I'm in no hurry. I am sorry, I don't know about you, Your Honours, but really ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric you gave us the impression last Friday that much as you like the Tribunal, you liked Bosnia-Herzegovina better and you were very anxious to get home and we are trying to facilitate you because we know that you through no fault of your own have had to sit around here for a long time doing nothing and we are trying to allow you to return to your family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, you are not answering and you should be aware that you are not answering questions for the Prosecutor or to the Prosecutor but the -- but for the Chamber, for the Judges, and you are bound to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the Chamber did not ask me any questions. But right, never mind, I'll answer, so this document was signed by the heads of my sectors, Dr. Toni Kolak, and Dr. Ivo Sandrk and I believe one of the locals who were there where they were. Now, I'm continuing the first part of my answer. Yes, I take great pride in this document, because here in the heading, it says, "After upon the completion of the outside investigation and execution of the orders, number such and such, dated 18th of August, 1993, and the 28th of August, 1993, regarding the implementation of provision of the international medication law prevention of infections and diseases and so on and so forth, I order," which means that this is clear evidence that we supervised the health care, the condition, of the war systematically and that therefore denied the right of anyone, including the Prosecutor, to create any doubts whether he asks such questions, "Didn't you do it this a little bit late in the day?" And I put it to you, Your Honours, Your Honours, the Presiding Judge and you two beautiful ladies, that there is a document, since dated early August --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, will you please warn the witness that he needs to slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you have to understand that the Prosecutor asked you a question which is very simple one, that is what's the name of that physician? And you answered this question. If the Prosecutor needs more explanations he will ask you the follow-up questions. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. President, before that, he asked me a highly provocative question and I also want to answer that question too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on whether we are interested in this question or not, Mr. Witness. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask the usher to show you please Exhibit P614.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I indicate that we did not comment on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have finished dealing with this document and whilst fully respecting your decision -- your decisions, my objections, I will voice at the end, and I will also request an investigation of this document because it shows that certain things were covered and rephotocopied. We here see a part of the stamp from somebody else. We can see a small part in the Croatian original. So obviously, there was some tampering with the photocopying and here in the English one, you will see under 1, it says, "Medical posts," and then it was shaded. So it was either crossed out or a piece of paper was put over it. It says that the source is the Zagreb archive but I keep looking and can't find that stamp on the Croatian original. And since we have for the first file a witness who is confirming the document, saying it does not complete, yes, where is the rest of the document and what is being done with this document? Where is these latter parts of this document? This is not the complete document. We are being shown here the documents today which is obviously not complete and somebody claims they are complete? How many documents of this kind have we had so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much to draw our attention to this document. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, although admittedly the copy is not as good as we would like it to be, in the upper left -- right corner, in the letterhead, there is the indication of a seal, from the HVO -- from the Zagreb archive. There is a round circle which looks exactly like the ones we have seen on hundreds of documents. I can also verify independently that according to our records, it came from the Zagreb archive. Let me suggest, respectfully, Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Krsnik jumps to conclusions for too quickly. The document could have easily xeroxed, perhaps it's never happened to Mr. Krsnik, I suspect it's happened to everyone else in the courtroom. Sometimes in you're copying documents if the documents are not laid flat on the copying machine you get a piece of the last document. I think Mr. Krsnik should not be so quick to claim forgeries and illegalities on the basis of absence of evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber will take into consideration the views expressed by both parties when we are making the decision on the admission of these documents. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you'll look next now, it's P614.1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, is it this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have the usher's assistance? We seem to have a lot of difficulty with the witness, it's Exhibit 614.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a communication dated the 29th of September, 1993, where Mr. Stanko Bozic, the director of the central military prison says, "Dear sir, I'm writing to you in order to inform you about the difficulties and problems regarding the medical treatment of certain number of seriously wounded persons, et cetera." Again we have lack of time here. Refers to the inadequate accommodation and the lack of material and medicaments. Forgive me if I've said that wrongly. Sir isn't it true that you're copied CC number 1, Brigadier Ivan Bagaric. Isn't it true, sir, that even by the end of September, conditions at the Heliodrom were not consistent with international or medical norms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to answer this question, I need the previous document. That is the document that I had before. Because it is also very important if I'm to it answer this question, the document that I just had, that incomplete document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they are looking for the document, I'll try to comment on this one. I told you that when, in an organised way, we entered the centre, I told you that it was in an organised way and I told you what we did there and why? Yes, of course, we constantly supervised the situation there and whatever it was, we requested that it be made better, that it be improved. Therefore, --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did Mr. --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was not the answer, I respect that the Chamber always tries to give the witness the opportunity to give a full explanation. The Chamber has given me one hour. This is not the question I asked. I didn't asked what steps were taken to improve the conditions. I said the conditions were not adequate. That was my question, at the end of September, 1993. I believe the witness has answered that question, at least in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we continuously supervised the state of health and the health care in the centres. In the report which I remember very well and which was written before this date, by our physicians, in that report, it says that the medicines are enough, that the state of health, the health, that is the state of health, was good. So that is that if treatment was required, it was provided. I cannot accept the assessment of Stanko Bozic, who is not a doctor and who takes it upon himself to comment on the state of health of the patients. So from that point of view, this document, to my mind, is irrelevant and unimportant, because it shows that Mr. Bozic took care of the wards and this is commendable, but he cannot assess how we had organised the health care. Your Honours, if you like, I can bring -- I don't know, because I didn't know, I didn't know that we will be going into this specific part of the problem, but I can gather the documentation and I'm at your disposal. For the full documentation, not only partial documentation, because from fragmented pictures, who are often the wrong ones, you cannot gain a proper picture. You will go astray. So that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you should answer that the medicines are enough and the state of the health was good. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if the medicine was good and the state of health was good, I take it you have no explanation for why Mr. Bozic on the 29th of September would be writing to you and saying, "The International Red Cross committee should not find out that they are accommodated in medically treated under inadequate conditions and consequently to create a bad impression about the central military prison as that could damage the HVO and as well as all Croatian people" what you're telling this Chamber is that Mr. Bozic had no basis, the head of the prison, the head of the prison, had no basis to make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document includes a sentence, at the same time, I'm asking you to transfer this group and ensure hospitalisation. So the gentleman had obviously sent this document to different places. He informed a number of people. I'm one of them. As for my part, he obviously wanted to transfer the sick, but a letter from him was not necessary for that, because we were doing that. The medical team which was there did that. So I think that this document is in order, meaning that Mr. Stanko Bozic obviously took care, I don't know, in the centre which he headed, took care, but his assessment about the state of health care, the medicine supply and all that is to me completely irrelevant because I have no reason to take Bozic's assessment -- to accept Bozic's assessment and not the assessment of my physicians. And I know that at the time, the physicians were reporting that everything was in order in so far as the health care organisation was concerned. And I claim this under full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Scott, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can we come to the end of that letter and say that as far as Dr. Bagaric is concerned, that letter is ill-informed and unfair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think when it comes to the assessment of health care and that aspect, I think that it simply does not provide the real picture. I claim that under full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Bagaric, I just want to ask Mr. Scott something while we are on the matter. Mr. Scott, I notice that the person who is described as the director of the central military prison on the 29th of September, 1993, is Mr. Stanko Bozic. And the document you referred us to about half an hour ago, 171.1, refers to a prison warden called Mr. Mile Pusic. Can you tell me, are they occupying the same role? Has there been a change of personnel or is Mr. Bozic senior to Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Clark, subject to verifying this, I can only say, if you'll allow me, based on the general knowledge of these matters that are I carry in my head, I think that by September of 1993, in fact earlier than that but certainly since September of 1992, Mr. Pusic had been replaced by Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution case that Mr. Bozic had been the chief administrator, if you like, of the Heliodrom for some considerable time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, who were the doctors, you said you put a great deal of stock in the doctors that reported to you. Can you give us some of the names again of these doctors?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Dr. Ivan Curic, specialist in "infectology" [as interpreted] -- He head the team. He was the head of the team which took care of this part. Also, Dr. Ivan Sandrk, that is Dr. Ivan Curic was the head for the preventive medicine in the medical corps head staff. Ivan Sandrk was head of the control and inspection. That is supervision of the quality of health work in the HVO units. And Dr. Toni Kolak, who at that time was a surgeon, and he headed the team which took care of the wounded.
