So my head down to Mr. Bozic and his care, but when it comes to the organisation of the health care there, then I place much more stock in them, in what they say, in what they testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, sir, so I want to be absolutely clear about this. When you refer to Dr. Ivan Curic, Dr. Toni Kolak -- I'm sorry if I pronounce, the pronunciation was wrong, and there was one more, Mr. Ivan Sandrk, you put great stock and credibility in the reports of those doctors, then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that lawyers are something completely different from the physicians. Physicians have no right to place stock or to trust anyone, and those people, and my relationship with them, was the guarantee, I had no reason to doubt that. I hear, I assume, all the responsibility here openly, I assume the responsibility if any of those physicians or any other physician subordinate to me did something wrong. I therefore personally assume the responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, our time is getting away from us. Would you please look at P618.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wish to warn Your Honours that this document is not complete either, nor full, because in the Croatian and English version, it says, "Annex, list of the wounded and sick." So this document is only part of another document containing the list. But the list is missing. So once again, we are dealing with an incomplete document. And who knows what that other part says?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the same objection we've made before. The document bears all the indications it bears. The Zagreb archive stamp, it bears a stamp of Mostar HVO stamp, it bears the signatures, apparent signatures, of at least two or three of the doctors on the last page of the Croatian version. If there is another attachment, we will certainly make every effort to provide it, Your Honour, but again, counsel is getting up before the witness has had a chance to give the answer the question and preempts, the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think Mr. Krsnik is talking about the document P614.1, the document we have used already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know, to be honest now, which one he's referring to, maybe Mr. Krsnik can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any way, we will take into consideration the views expressed by both parties at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir would you look at 618.1? And sir, according to this document it is a report from three of the very doctors that you just named.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On item number 1 on touring the centre, we were not stopped or asked for identity papers by authorised officials. Two, there is an insufficient number of persons physically guarding the centre. Three, the centre surroundings and the centre itself are messy and neglected. Four, the centre is overcrowded with inmates. Five, the centre's surgery is well supplied with medicines and medical supplies. Six, the surgery's working hours are from 0 to 24 hundred hours, there are two doctors, four nurses and one assistant pharmacist working in the surgery. Seven, there is no segregation in centre between the wounded, sick and healthy inmates. Eight, the hygienic conditions are absolutely unsatisfactory and there was a great likelihood of an outbreak of intestinal and respiratory diseases. Sir, those are the conclusions of the three doctors you told us a moment ago you found to be credibility and their signatures are on the document. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the previous document that I said was signed by them, by the three of them, will you give me the document, please? That is I know about these documents because I carry them here in my head because they are important to me. I signed this document but this other part is missing. Give me the document. The first time when I said that these three signed, I meant that other document. Give me, please, that document, the previous one, that incomplete document which is my document. My apologies. So this is how it is. This is clear evidence, this is clear evidence corroborating what I said. So this is the team, Kolak, Sandrk, Ivan Curic, so that is my team. They entered and toured the prison, the centre. So from item 1 to item 8, not a single item refers to any criticism of the health care, from item 1 to item 7. Just a moment. Meaning that item 5 confirms what I said, that the centre is well supplied with medicines and medical supplies. That there is no segregation in the centre, that the clinic works 24 hours. So nothing of this is a criticism. Why, the contrary, it confirms that we organised the service well. Item 8, Mr. Lawyer, the hygienic conditions are not -- don't have -- don't have to be provided and need not be provided by the health personnel. So I'm talking about the hygienic, the sanitary conditions. That is what I'm talking about, that includes cleanliness, regular baths, and prevention and so on and so forth. So only this particular item qualifies to be as the only possible source of danger. And after that inspection, straight away, we wrote an order, a new order, I'm giving it to you, which had to do with how to prevent these events. So this document is another document that I take pride in and which is proof that we systematically and in an organised way embarked on the solution of this problem and solved it. There is also the measures which we proposed and it says, act according to order so of the 28th of September, 1993, and it probably says, I don't know it by heart, that more cutlery and crockery sets be brought, that these vessels be washed better and so on and so forth to prevent infectious diseases and that we worked well is also confirmed that there was no infection. It did not take place, Mr. Honourable Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So sir, by what you've told us in the last few minutes that we can take that exhibit as being absolutely accurate and you're proud of it, whatever it says in that exhibit, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First part of the document absolutely, but the second part is missing, and that part was signed by me. That is a document that I signed. So you cannot deal with my papers which are not complete. What I am telling you is that you can't do that. I have to explain that that's why I have to go on explaining to you because you don't have complete documents. Why didn't you ask for these documents from me? I would have given them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could please show you Exhibit P638.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just a moment, could I clarify something while we are looking at it, is what you're saying that your letter of the 28th of September, 1993, that's called an order, and we called it Exhibit 612.2, is the attachment to that last document we were dealing with, 618.1? Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately no. Can I please have all the document that is I've seen so far? I will place them in a proper order because I know the order. I'm referring to the document that I first claimed were signed by -- I understand you. I understand why you're confused. I also need time but I will demonstrate why. This document, there is just one page, and on that page it says, "Order." This is a document for which I first claimed that it was signed by Kolak, Sandrk and others, but they did not. This document was signed by me. I did not have the second part. That's what confused me. But then when the gentleman showed me another paper which indeed was signed by the three people, this has made me conclude that this -- how things happened. So this is the date is 28 September, 1993, but it says in this document that after the inspection on site, an order issued on 18 and 20 August, 1993, with regard to the application of the provisions of the humanitarian law and so on and so forth so there were other prior documents, orders, which were issued by me on the proposal of my colleagues, doctors whom I always trusted. So I issued these orders on their recommendation. So this is just one in a series of orders designed for setting up proper medical care that we would all be satisfied with. But we were never satisfied. There was always room for improvement. We strived for more. And one of the problems was malnourishment but we could not provide enough food for the people. Somebody else was in charge of that. International organisations which did not supply people with enough food. We had to feed the refugees as well, unfortunately. If you need these documents, and if they will clarify some things for you, I can send them to you, Your Honours, and they will be more complete for to you have a full insight, because these are just fragments in the mosaic and fragments don't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, let's come to the DP138.1. Mr. Scott, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a report to Mr. Bruno Stojic on eleventh of October, 1993, concerning the Heliodrom prison. Sorry -- sorry, my colleague is pointing out that in the transcript we may have a wrong reference, the exhibit is P638.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric I'm not going to direct your attention to it items under the first page at this point, the use of detainees for work. I direct your attention to item number 2, on the second page, or -- well, I don't know if it's the second page of your -- yes, it is the second page, severe wounding and other sufferings of the detainees. Mr. Bozic reports 2(a) a large number of wounded detainees need the kind of medical attention that can only be administered at a hospital which we are unable to provide. The problem of the -- (b), the problem of the supply of medical equipment, medicines and basic items for personal hygiene, his remark under (c), international committee of the red cross visited the central investigative prison on the 10, 11th and 12th of August and pointed out a number of irregularities that also constitute violations of the Geneva Conventions, including (a), (b) and (c). Now, sir, I put it to you again is it not true that as time progressed into the fall of 1993, the conditions at the Heliodrom, the medical conditions, the conditions of confinement, still do not comply with international or medical norms, did they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I comment upon all the allegations written by Mr. Bozic? I believe this to be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but do it as concisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under (a), the sentence ends in which we are unable to provide. If Mr. Bozic was not able to provide this, and if this document is authentic, then it was us, doctors, who were able to provide it, for all, irrespective of who the wounded was, to which side he belonged, if they were wounded, they were sent to the hospital. If we were informed about that, if we had contact with the wounded. Under (b), the problem of the supply of medical equipment, medicines and basic items for personal hygiene, that was the problem that we had across the board of the entire organisation of the health care of the HVO. We had that in the hospital in Mostar. That was the problem. But that problem was tackled and shared with the units, and in the same way, the units were supplied with medicines, it was very difficult because supplies were very scarce, and we -- within our possibilities, we supplied sufficient quantities of those to the investigation centre. The problem existed but we dealt with it. Under (c), there is a need for setting up and so on and so forth. He says that there is a need to set up a dispensary. A commission, our commission, proposed that a medical centre should be established, as a point, and this was done. As far as I know, I believe that this medical centre even had beds for possible cases, but these were absolutely irrelevant in this context because whoever needed treatment and they would be brought to the hospital for treatment. And I will finish with the remark, the International committee and so on and so forth, three comments, (a), (b), (c), none of these comments is relative to health care as health care, as such. I already mentioned early on that the quality of food was questionable, food rations were very insufficient, there was not enough food. As for the quality and quantity of food, I cannot comment. As for the use of detainees for work, I don't know, I cannot comment upon that, because I've been talking about the organisation of health care and I can only answer questions in that sense. So here I don't see a single allegation which would deny my testimony with regard to the organisation of health care. This is what I've -- I tried to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is a bit confused and that's why I need your assistance. What is the document that we are currently talking about? I apologise, doctor, I thought we were looking at 638.1. Is that the document that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I have a totally different content. That's why I'm confused, whatever the doctor has been talking about, I don't have. None of these items in document 638.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you the only one with this problem? Do you know where it is? On the second page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I can't find the document. The right document. I understand the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the number is 01540561 in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, since there is no substantial objections from the Defence counsel, you may proceed while the Defence counsel will find the proper page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention first of all to exhibit -- I can't deal with it without the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krsnik is right, if you look at the B/C/S version, there seems to be a page missing. There is certainly one missing from mine if you look at it compared with the translation, there is a paragraph 1 which goes from (a) to (e) and then the next page is paragraph 6 whereas there are several paragraphs with (a), (b), (c), on the English version, so I think Mr. Krsnik probably has an inadequate version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've obviously spent more time looking at the document in the last few minutes than I have. I can only compare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Judge Lieu has pointed out it's not in the correct sequence but it's there, the second page is after the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it is, Your Honour, and I apologise, mine is not stapled that way, but these things do happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask the usher's an assistance showing you 661.11? Directing your attention to the Croatian language original, sir, which is the document -- does the document bear your name in type? And bear a -- a hand marking, I won't necessarily I won't call it necessarily a signature, initials and some hand marking and to the left of that, the Herceg-Bosna stamp? Yes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that your name and that marking yours, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indeed my name. The -- I did not initial, this is not my initial but I believe this is an authentic document. I don't remember this document. There was a number of such documents, but I believe this is our authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So directing your attention to item numbered 2, did you not say on that date, the 27th of October, 1993, the ordered PMZ, prevention and medical protection measures had been inspected and checked in the Heliodrom and Gabela centre, the ordered PMZ measured have not be implemented and have been urgently ordered to remover the faults. So in fact, sir, even by the end of October, these corrections had not been made, according to your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, all the documents that they have brought are clear evidence of what I have been talking about, that we have systematically looked after everything. Under item 1, sanitary inspection of the Grude ONP has been carried out, under 2, the ordered PMZ prevention medical protection measures, have been inspected and checked in the Heliodrom and Gabela. The ordered PMZ measures have not been fully implemented, full stop. You forgot to read the rest of it. It has been urgently ordered to remove the faults. And so on and so forth. So we continuously entered, supervised and continuously were dissatisfied. What does this mean? I have to clarify. Because the way you may be interpreting it is that nothing was done there. We wanted more to be done. We saw a room for an epidemics to break out. That's why we intervened, that's why no epidemics broke out. If you were to inspect the hotel where I am actually staying, which is a four-star hotel, I hope that they are not going to it hear what I'm going to it say in a minute, but if you were to control that hotel, I'm sure you would come across something, some faults that need to be changed in order to improve things. So Mr. Prosecutor, in a detention centre, in a city where it is not sure that you will be alive on the following day, in which the war is being waged, in which we do the control, which we carry out supervision, and we propose some things, I think we should be commended. I fully expect the Prosecutor could commend me on doing the job well, the job that we were in charge with and that we belong to a unit which was in no way a unit of -- consisting of criminals, so if I was a good doctor, if my doctors were good, if the whole unit was good, why should not we be commended, in Hitler's time even doctors did evil things, so I do not understand, Mr. Prosecutor, what you are trying to prove with this. This I am very proud of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention, sir, to Exhibit 697.1?, to conclude, Your Honour, I have this exhibit and one more exhibit and even though by no means is my examination truly completed, I can represent to the Chamber a number of interesting topics, but after the conclusion -- after those two exhibits, I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there any English translations for this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour. 697.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we have been furnished with them, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, can I just say one sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, one sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I protest against the Prosecutor's sentence that he has a few more things to show us but he will be brief, because there is no more time. I ask him to continue. I don't want to leave this place feeling that there were other things but there was no time. This is very important. You should find time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I believe that it is the Chamber who will conduct the cross-examination of this trial. We decide how long the Prosecution will have. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to read this entire document to you because we don't have time. But it is another document that you prepared, is it not true, sir, dated the 26th of November, 1993? We are now, sir, have gone probable approximately a month later at the end of November, and is it not true, sir, that still at that time, which is reflected by this document, the medical and health conditions, conditions of confinement, at the HVO detention centres were still not consistent with international law norms or medical norms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. Please tell me, I apologise, Your Honours, please tell me what makes you allege again the same thing? If I told you that we were continuously working and supervising? So this document dating 26th November, was addressed to Dr. Drago Dzambas and refers to the entire area, and I repeat, I did not read this document, I cannot remember any document from that time but this is another proof that we repeatedly wanted and strived to improve, to control, the health care of the detainees, and I will answer your question. Not even in the hospitals of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this moment, the situation of health care is not the way it should be. That is my answer, at this very moment, as we speak, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you say in this letter, upon the completion, you refer back to the earlier documents that we looked at this afternoon based on the on site investigation on the 28th of August, 1993. It is now some three months later. And you report this in the terms of things to be done. In the last paragraph of your report, you state, "The above mentioned must be understood as a priority and a permanent task." I put it to you, sir, with that because I do have to conclude, according to the Chamber's guidelines, so the conditions of the camp never substantially improved, they became a matter of international outrage and it was only after the pressure of the Republic of Croatia that these camps were closed at the end of 1993. Now, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am glad that finally you recognise that the Republic of Croatia did something good in Bosnia-Herzegovina after all. What you have just said is not true. It is nothing but, let me put it this way, it is not correct. I have been able to demonstrate with the continuity of my documents, but not all of them, but those that you have had at your disposal that we continuously monitored the situation and supervised the situation of the detainees and whenever we were there and we were there all the time, we strived for more. And imagine if I had not issued this paper at all? Does that mean, Mr. Prosecutor, that in that case, our health care would be good? This is just to prove that we worked continuously, that we strived for more. And when you say that with time, the situation went from bad to worse, is a lie. With time, the situation improved. Your Honours, what I can now wonder is whether there was time when we could all do more, where I could do more. Then the answer is yes. That was immediately after this prison was opened. And this is the period where I could discuss here the things that we failed to do. But after that, with time, the situation only improved, and nobody in their right mind can prove to the contrary. So it is simply a lie to say that the situation was either the same or worse. And that has absolutely nothing to do with the closing down of these centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your next document, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Direct our attention sir to P716.1. We seem to have lost the usher. Oh, sorry, I didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to respect the principles of my duty. I know that I enjoy the trust of this Court and Judge Clark has often warned me that I have to have trust in this Chamber and I do, again this document is being misinterpreted in the cross-examination. It is being interpreted as a letter or a report. It is an order. What needs to be done all over the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this is being misinterpreted -- misrepresented during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another very brief explanation, if I may, please. I thank my -- the counsel. This refers to the entire area, and the documents that we had before me earlier were -- referred to the centres. So this is another proof -- Your Honours, how can I know what went on in Central Bosnia if I couldn't get there? And this letter is addressed to a doctor in Central Bosnia, so this letter applied to him as well. And in so far as we had information from him. This is just -- the Prosecutor has -- is just setting me up and I'm really sorry, Mr. Prosecutor, that you have -- you are resorting to these means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Usher, did you find that document? Yes? Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any objections, just to provide for the just treatment of both sides in these proceedings, I am bound by my conscience and the protection of my client, I need to say that the Prosecutor has used more time than was allowed for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution has realised the time he used. He tried to wind up his cross-examination by using the last document. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in referring you to Exhibit P716.1, do you recall, sir, looking at this document, that there was a decision by Mate Boban dated around the 10th of December, 1993, to close the following HVO detention camps? Gabela, Heliodrom, Ljubuski, Livno, Tomislavgrad and Prozor detention camps? That's my first question. Do you remember the order of Mate Boban to close all those camps at the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course I don't remember. I didn't work in Mate Boban's office, I didn't work in detention centres so I don't know. If this document is accurate, what is in it that I should remember it by?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll close with this: I just put it to you just as a matter of record that we are required to do this and there may be other evidence that the Chamber has heard or will here: Isn't it true, sir, that these camps were closed because the conditions in the camps, the conditions of the inmates, medical conditions, the hygienic conditions, the conditions of confinement, had become a matter of international outrage and only on the pressure received from the government of Croatia were these camps closed at the end of 1993? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for interpretation to end to make it easier for my colleagues. Your Honours, I believe this is inadmissible. The Prosecutor constantly appropriate certain rights and I suppose he thinks he has more rights than we do, that he is the lord and master of this Court. He may not testify in this manner. This is not cross-examination. I would not be allowed to do that certainly. These -- this is the testimony by the Prosecutor, it is not a question, nor is it pursuing an answer, nor does he want an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I really frankly speaking, I really could not understand you. I could not understand your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour may I -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we will hear from Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rule 90, rule 90, section (h)(2) states quote, "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "... for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to the witness the nature of the case, of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." And I put my case, I've closed the -- I'm attempt to go meet the Chamber's guidelines as best I can on the time and I'm closing by putting our case very clearly to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not what was read out from the Rules because we know the Rules, but the Prosecutor asked a question and provided an answer. To make such claims true, he's got his indictment which he needs to prove. And these allegations he needs to prove because he's got a document. We are not here to prove the innocence. The burden is on him to prove the guilt. And for such words in the phrasing of questions, and providing an immediate answer by using some allegations which he has failed to prove so far, it is inadmissibility in cross-examination, sorry, I may be wrong and that is why I addressed the Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I don't see anything wrong with this question. Frankly speaking, this procedure has been practised in this Tribunal for many cases, and we have been sitting here for almost a year. I don't see anything wrong from the Prosecution to ask a question like this. And I have to emphasise that your witness has the full right to rebut any case put to him in front of us, the Judges, and we will make the proper assessment of all the witnesses or testimonies given by this witness. There is no problem about that. I understand you do not agree with what the Prosecution said as a conclusion. It's quite understandable. But the Prosecution has the full right to put his case to this witness. And this witness has the full right to answer this question or deny any allegations. I don't see anything wrong, frankly speaking, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that I acted to the detriment of my client, then I didn't know how to do my business in my cross-examination, because at that time, while respecting the equality of arms I was entitled whenever I had witnesses for the Prosecution, whenever I realised they were not telling the truth about the Heliodrom because they could not identify the buildings, I could put it to them, I put it to you that you've never been to Heliodrom and you know nothing about it, but I never did that because I thoughts I was not allowed to, because I wanted to treat decently victims and conditionally calling witnesses and so on and so forth. And I'm now saying that I acted prejudicially to my client because my defence was then wrong and I'm not ashamed to admit that in public because that is not how I behaved, nor did I say that nor did I put such allegations to the witnesses for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, if you believe that your cross-examination is not adequate, and if you believe that there are certain points which are very essential to the Defence of your client, the Rules have provided you with an opportunity at the later stage, that is the rebuttal and rejoinder procedures. Yes, Mr. Seric? We have spent a lot of time on procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true, Mr. President, and I apologise, but I object to this question for a completely different reason. Namely my client, Vinko Martinovic, that is the question is completely irrelevant and out of place because he's not responsible for the setting up of prisons or the treatment and guarding of prisoners, not a single one, so I do not know what this question, what this Prosecutor's question has to do with the charges against my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand that this witness is for Mr. Naletilic. Yes, Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the Prosecutor. I understand that Mr. Prosecutor, of course, needs to persist in his intent and in some way discredit me as a witness. That is how I understand it. All this time, that was his approach, that is how I saw them. However, I do not see where has he proven that my affirmations were inaccurate in this regard. So my answer to this question is as follows: All the detention centres, prisons or I don't know what in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were regrettably contrary to the interests, contrary to the interests of Croats and Muslims Bosniaks, so they were closed down in the interests and to the benefit of both. Whoever contributed to that closure did a good job. Therefore, I withdraw my last sentence. In the prisons, in these centres or prisons or whatever you care to call them, the conditions were not such, when it comes to the health care, the conditions were not such as the Prosecutor is saying, and they cannot be related to that. It was simply a political decision to close them down. And of course, nobody enjoyed being there, wherever you might be detained. So I deny, I refute, any suspicion, any doubt or attempt to say that in my testimony I said something wrongly or interpreted something wrongly. I refute that absolutely, and I am at your disposal fully to prove that, to comment on that, and that is my answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate the Chamber's patience this afternoon. That concludes my questions. I think I would like to make a record, Your Honour, that among the topics, and I say among because it's not all of them, that I was not able to pursue, were the use of Muslim prisoners in forced labour, which I believe there are documents that would go to this witness, and also to the fact that a Herceg-Bosna war crimes commission was established in November 1993 to which the witness was named which I think would be an interesting topic for the Chamber, the war crimes commission, but we have not had time to go into those topics. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 6.00. After that, we will do the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Your re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will endeavour to be very brief. We have just received the Croatian translation of P66.4 -- P566.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, can you tell us if your health care service, the points that you had at the Heliodrom, did you make any lists of persons, because according to this document that was put before you by the Prosecutor, it says that there were -- it indicates the number of persons. Did you have the exact information about the number of people in the central investigative prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there the first time, the information I was given was that it was a large number of detained or incarcerated, of inmates, and I thought that that was that. I mean, a large number. Several thousand or something. And I believe I even used once that many people had been incarcerated, and so on. But later on, when talking with the people who supervised the health care in the centre itself, I heard from them that that figure was too high, that -- but it was a large number, and they were saying there could have been up to 2.000 men. I don't know. Unfortunately I cannot give you the exacts number and at this moment I do not have the exact information so anything I give would be guessing, but that number was certainly not the one -- that I assumed for a while, that I was afraid was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell us, please, since the doctors had to provide medicines and the health care, did they inform you in their reports that that number changed, say July, August, September? Was the number always the same or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these questions which require exact, accurate figures. Unfortunately I cannot answer them precisely. What I do know with certainty, for instance, I remember that there was immediately a proposal that everybody over 60 or 65 should be let go. And all those under the age of 18. For instance, those who were younger. So on a number of occasions, in conversations, in talks, or based on proposals of I don't know, even our doctors, for instance, when somebody was ill and so on and so forth, that figure varied, yes, their number changed and, yes, of course, I don't know, but it varied from time to time, but I really cannot give you the exact figures because -- sorry, because I did not even have the information that we would be discussing this subject. So that I would have to refresh my contacts, check and see, and unfortunately, right now, I cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right, sorry, my last question, then. I appreciate what you are telling us and I thank you if you are not positive about something, if you do not have personal information but do you know if Dr. Curic would be able to provide us with that information? Does he know more than you do because he went there more often than you did?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, right. Like this. Yes, of course he has more information, but I have to say that neither Dr. Curic nor any other physician had primarily -- were responsible primarily, were tasked primarily with something related to figures. They were tasked with doing what needed to be done and that is extend the health care, so Dr. Curic of course will have more information, just as he will have more information about the health care itself. But of course, one can discuss the matter with the commanders themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. You know, in this courtroom we heard figures from 5.000 to 10.000, that is why I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, right, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, I have two more questions in relation to the documents. Her Honour Judge Clark asked you, you didn't answer not because you didn't want to but because my learned friend moved on to it a different answer and that answer took sometime. When Judge Clark asked you and the document is P612.2, which also incorporated the report signed by -- by the three doctors, it says that order of the health sector of the 28th of September, 1993. So Judge Clark asked you if that was an integral part, and you never had time to answer.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what you're talking about because I can remember that text. After -- after they had taken stock of the situation there regarding the health care, they also attached an earlier document so that it became part and parcel of that document making for an integral document. And along side this document, which they had made themselves, they attached yet another document. So that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This order that you issued on the 20th of September, 1993, should be an integral part of this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We did not get did it in this way, that's why I asked you that. And my very last question, witness, will you please be so kind and tell us, it is document P661.11, it is the document, you will remember, that the Prosecutor asked you if it was a facsimile?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could the usher please help me, will you look at the upper right corner and tell us if you had identify the signature and is it a common thing to have these doodles or signatures or initials in the upper part of the document? I'm referring to the upper part of the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: This is -- this can be a document forwarded by our headquarters elsewhere to somebody else, and that somebody else possibly initialed it in the upper part to indicate that he had received it. I'm guessing, I cannot make even an assumption. And this first part perhaps and this second part is something I do not understand, but this first part could even be Mr. Stojic's. It could be. So I go back to that part, whether the document was signed or not, which is what the Prosecutor asked me. Right. So if we -- when we made a document, we'd send this document to somewhere it was supposed to be sent but we could print out a copy of that same document and keep it for ourselves, so it did not have to be signed necessarily nor did it have to leave our office with this facsimile in the upper right corner, I say possibly that the person who received the document somewhere initialed it because, I assume, you got these documents from the archive of the Ministry of Defence and perhaps these documents were addressed to that ministry, perhaps I say. I cannot really say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us cut it short. Which document is considered original? After all the attempts to arrive at an answer, will you please tell us what is the original? For example this document, what does this document's original look like?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well, well, it has the heading which is the official heading, therefore, which is not like this one of course, which has a stamp and a signature, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you say signature, what kind of a signature do you mean? Because it is deemed here or there is an attempt to consider a signature, once typed signature?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, this here is machine. This is not the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Wait. You are making too much haste. When you say signature, do you mean a signature in one's own hand?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you mean this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm talking generally about an original document. What does an original of a document look like which you will says in the original?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yours.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my document, the originals of my documents were the ones which had down there the assistant of the head of the Defence Department, of course this is typed. And then this is signed either personally by myself personally or it is signed by one of my colleagues with me knowing who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And that is then considered the original document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my mind, yes, because otherwise we could not function. I could not be always present there and sign every document in my own hand so it always said, Ivan Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But doctor, if you're sending this document to the United Nations will you send it without your original signature?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is not a document that was addressed to the United Nations, this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about this document in particular, I'm asking you about documents in general that you created?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course I signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. And my last question, doctor, if the Defence asked you to, in to fortnight or roughly in a fortnight, if you could provide certain documentation and give it to the Defence so that I could file it with the Honourable Court, if that is possible, I don't know if you are prepared to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. A request from this Court is an obligation, that is how I see it. So of course I will do my utmost and provide whatever I can, primarily with my colleagues, with the doctors, to do that. Now, when I can do it, I really cannot say right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Thank you very much for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Dr. Bagaric, I'm hoping you'll clear up a few things for me. Prior to the conflict in 1992, even with the Serbs, what was the ethos of the main hospital in Mostar? Now, the word ethos may cause you some problems in translation. I don't know if it does. In many countries, well, in most countries -- you understand what ethos means?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I do. That's the national composition of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: No, doctor, in most countries I am familiar with, there are many religions operating in the country. Some of the hospitals have a Catholic ethos and maybe nuns run them. Some of the hospitals are Protestant and are run by a board, some are Jewish, looking at America and Britain, and some are run by a board of directors. That's what ethos means, that it leans towards the philosophy of a particular religion. In other words if it was a Catholic hospital would you have no terminations or probably no in vitro fertilisation, that sort of thing, there's ethos and ethics involved. Now the question I'm asking was the main hospital in Mostar which subsequently became the war hospital, did that hospital, prior to the conflict, have any particular ethos? Was it Catholic or Muslim or Orthodox or did it serve the entire population of the Mostar municipality? You're nodding. So it had no specific ethos, it served everybody. Good. When the HVO was set up, were there any flags flying outside the hospital then at that stage, when the HVO took over the day-to-day running, administration, of Mostar? Did the flag fly outside that hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I understand what you're saying, but I cannot say anything about the time immediately before the conflict in 1992, because I was not in Mostar, in that year. That was the time of conflict between Croats and Muslims on one side and Serbs on the other side. So I can truthfully not say anything about that, whether there was something or not, but what I can say, for a fact, is that during the conflict with the Muslims, so the conflict between Croats and Muslims, on several occasions, I pointed to the fact that not only -- not on the hospital, I did not see a Croatian flag on the hospital, but at a checkpoint in the courtyard of the hospital, within the perimeter of the hospital, at the very entrance where the military police controlled the entrance, I think I saw a Croatian flag on one occasion, and I intervened personally and I asked for that flag to be removed because it provided an excuse for possible shelling or I said that somebody may perceive it as a sign that we did not receive people of other affiliation or religion. So on the hospital itself I did not see a flag and I don't believe that there was one. The only flag was a red cross flag but I remember my personal intervention that took place within the perimeter of the hospital at the main entrance which was 300 or 500 metres away from the main building of the hospital. That's where the military police was checking the entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question I wanted to ask you is if the usher would be kind enough to furnish Dr. Bagaric with Exhibit D1/380? It's a list of medical supplies in a consignment for the BH Army dated the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I was just wondering, doctor, if you could explain to me what the initials "SC," which appear after quantities, what "SC" means?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "SC" I believe is a "scatula," that's a box. That's Latin, scatula, that's a box which contains medicines. So that's the abbreviation for scatula, so that's a measure for quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just wondered about that because the very last item, number 25 is called loose medicaments, two boxes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that these medicines such as penbritin under 1, so this is an antibiotic, it is listed and counted in scatulas. Now, loose medicaments, this could be infusions -- no, 24 is infusions solutions. That's one pallet. That is about 100 infusions. And as for loose medicaments and boxes, I don't understand. Maybe this means that there were a number of different medicaments which were not sorted for type because that's very often how we receive it. We received it in humanitarian aid. We still have a lot of medicaments from humanitarian aid which are poisoned because they are out of their date. So I think that these may be medicaments which are not assorted or sorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. I leave that aside now. Doctor, from what I understand of your testimony, correct me if I'm wrong, is that prior to July, mid-July, 1993, you were unaware of the existence or the operation of the Heliodrom as a detention centre for Muslims, that when you went there, there was no medical care being provided at all.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be completely precise, the first time I heard about the detainees at the meeting in Jablanica that I mentioned earlier on, then Mr. Halilovic mentioned that there were detained soldiers, although the war had not even started yet, and I was really surprised, and indeed one commission visited that prison which was there and I didn't even know where Heliodrom was, and people were released. That's number 1. Number 2, during the conflict, in the month of May and June, I told you that in June, in mid-June, I went where I went, that was Canada. When I returned, I believe it was sometime in mid-June, so I left towards the end of June and I returned in mid-June. Or around the 20th of June. Then I heard from other doctors that they had entered these premises, that those who required help were receiving treatment, and then I heard about a huge number of people, and that we were supposed to intervene, and then I also told you how I contributed towards that intervention. That was my initial visit together with Dr. Lang that I already told you about. But at that time, I can't tell you for a fact that this or that person supervised this or that. But I know that chiefs of medical services of particular brigades in the area received people and provided them with care. And from the -- from my visit onwards, we established a continuous, organised protection and supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, can I take it that your evidence, then, is that whatever care prisoners had before your visit towards the end of July, 1993, following your visit there with Dr. Lang, the service improved?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Because we've heard from Mr. Bruno Stojic when gave evidence -- did I say something that I should not say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, Your Honour, but Mr. Bruno Stojic never gave evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, who was the gentleman who was in a very high position? He may be a protected witness. Maybe I should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're referring to Mr. Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Forgive me, we have terrible problems with referring these names. This gentleman who was in a position of importance in the HVO went to visit the Heliodrom and he told us that he was shocked by what he saw, but I believe that he may well have gone before you went, that that may be the situation. But any way, your evidence is that after your visit, there was a material improvement in the health care afforded to these prisoners. Now, the question I want to ask is, Dr. Bagaric, do you make a distinction in function between the general welfare of the detainees and the care of the detainees when their medical condition gave rise to such a necessity? Do you make a distinction between welfare and medical care?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line is very thin between the two. People cannot be provided with good health care and be malnourished at the same time. I know what you're saying. When you ask me whether the condition improved after our visit, the completely correct answer would be as follows. I don't believe that it improved on the following morning or even within two or three days, but a few days later, ten days later, it improved significantly because we insisted on doctors going there. And then at the beginning of August, we even organised our medical point within that centre, and I agree with you that the conditions that prevailed there, the overpopulated conditions, obviously aggravated the overall condition of these people and also meant a lot of problems for the health care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You made a distinction, doctor, between the sanitary problems, the lack of toilet facilities, washing facilities. I take it you could do nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something that falls under the logistics which were necessary in order to provide for certain conditions. That is the sanitary inspection which has to be carried out in order to provide for the conditions that would prevent the breaking out of any epidemics, I immediately I can tell you that our results were not spectacular at the beginning but after the opening of our centre, the situation even with that improved and as a result of that, there were no epidemics. There was no serious health condition seen in a number of people. And if you read all the items of the document that the Prosecution has provided you with, especially the second page, where it says that the chlorine has to be added to the water, that stools of those who were handling food have to be inspected, that the diet has to be improved, that the hygiene has to be improved, washing and so on and so forth,. Obviously conditions were very serious and could not be good, could not be optimal conditions, but from my point of view, as a doctor, what was necessary that everybody who needed health care should be provided with health care and that the break out of epidemics were prevented and that those who had to be referred to hospitals should be referred to hospitals. And we succeeded in doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. It knew you may feel that this is outside of your area of expertise or your knowledge but I'll ask you the question because we are concerned about it. In the year that you were in Mostar and that really was the time when the worst hostilities were going on, in 1993, were you ever personally aware as a doctor and in the position you had in the HVO, that there were reports, I won't put it any more than that, there were reports that prisoners were being used on the front line or near the front line, and as a result, a number of them sustained gunshot injuries or were killed. Were you personally aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that people would go out to do some works, groups of people would be engaged in works, so due to the scarcity in the -- of workforce, people were sent out to do some work. Whether that was some sort of labour or work, I don't know. I heard of that. But where they were taken, where they were, where they were injured and how, I can't tell you with full certainty. I think that it would be good if you could establish contacts with those people who were there. I'm sure that they could provide you with a lot more information. I did hear that people from these centres were taken to do some work and that they were injured and I also heard that some of them were even killed. Now, for me to speculate whether this happened in this or in another way, there was a lot of shelling going on, I can't say anything about that, I can't give my testimony to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can you help me with this, then, doctor? Was it any part of your duty or any part of your portfolio in relation to the position that you held, to direct an investigation into the death of a prisoner? Was that something that was done by the police or did you have any role at all in that, if a prisoner were to die or a prisoner were to be badly injured, was there any protocol for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody were to be injured, then they would be treated in the hospital and as a patient. The destiny of these people from then on was their destiny in the hospital. And they received the same treatment as everybody else, and the hospital had its principle, its structures of work, and I did not have the need to intervene. I did not have any objections about the health care extended to the injured persons, no matter of their religion, Muslim, Croats, that was not my authority and I did not need to intervene. As -- when somebody was killed, these centres had their respective commanders and I told you that our doctors were in the centre in charge, i.e. it was my duty to provide the maximum level of health care. We could not assume responsibility for the fact whether the people were taken for work or not, and whether they were going to be injured there or not. A few days ago, I told you that we were very surprised to see these centres because we were in no way prepared. So my main task was to organise health care for the units and for the population. So when these centres were opened, we provided health care there because there was nobody else to provide health care. I'm afraid that international organisations did not enough to increase their presence. So when I talked about our proposals, when that representatives of the Red Cross have to be present there, all the time, in order to report on the conditions in these centres, that was my proposal. So -- what you asked me was not in -- under our authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could you help us with this, doctor? Whose authority would the treatment of prisoners of war or detainees come under? Who was responsible for the welfare of detainees who were injured or who were killed? We know from documents that we've seen, doctor, that there were detainees who were injured and killed. I'm not saying who caused the injuries or how they were killed, but we know that while they were on day release from the hospital, because there are records that show that, that they sustained injuries close to or at the confrontation line. Who would have been responsible for the welfare of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about those instances when somebody was injured. Either a detainee or anybody else. Then it was our responsibility. So it was either -- it was medical service, the hospital. When it came to those people who were killed, it was not our responsibility. We were not responsible for the Croatian Defence Council, for civilians or for members of the HV army or anybody else. Later on, there were some bodies which looked after the victims of war but this certainly fell beyond the scope of our authority. I apologise. Those who were injured and who were treated, that was under our authority. These people were treated in our hospitals. I can't tell you here that everybody who was injured was treated by us. We did treat them, if they were brought to the institution, if we knew about them, but if our member of the HVO or somebody else were injured somewhere where doctors were not present, where it was very remote and doctors never knew about it and somebody could bleed to death without any assistance being extended to them because roads were blocked or that person was not pulled out in due course, and the help just did not arrive on time but all those that we admitted, that our services and our hospitals admitted, we were responsible for those people who had been injured, we were responsible for their treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, if I could sum up your evidence as I understand it, in relation to that aspect of your evidence, the facilities were there for the treatment of all injured people no matter what background they came from, but that there was nothing that you or your doctors could do to make the military bring them to the hospital for treatment. That was outside of your area of responsibility. You could provide the treatment but you couldn't force anybody to bring the injured detainees for treatment.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any case that somebody was injured and needed help and was not brought in and was not treated. So your allegation that there is a possibility that something like that may have happened, unfortunately is not true. I just want you and me to clarify one thing. What I said was that there may have been an HVO soldier who was injured in one of those, so to say, pockets or enclaves and people there could not bring the injured person to a medical centre in time, and that is why somebody may have lost their lives. I know of such cases. I remember a case of a medical -- of a nurse who was killed from an ambush and by the time they had found her, she was still alive but she -- she actually bled to death. As a rule, I never heard of anybody who was injured, regardless of their background, who was not transported to where they had to be transported to. What I'm saying is that sometimes, they arrived too late. If you are referring specifically to those people who were doing some work, they were detainees, I never heard of anybody like that being injured and not being brought in. I really have -- did not hear of any such case. So what I believe is that whoever was injured or wounded, regardless of their nationality was treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still at the Heliodrom. Let us talk about the Heliodrom. And you said that this, the Heliodrom, that this camp was an undesirable result of the war. I liked that feeling. But what we need to know is were you indignant because of the conditions under which they were detained, that is lack of room, lack of heating, lack of sanitary conditions, so on and so forth, or were these people in a deplorable state of health? Were there any general illnesses, infectious diseases, contagious diseases or some other, some inflammations and if that happened as a result of running a gauntlet, of beating, of this or that, that is I think that you were very vague when you spoke, and in spite of the explanations thaw provided to my colleague, I'd really like to know precisely what was it that made you indignant about it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. To begin with, when I said the result of the war, that is an undesirable outcome, I meant that specifically or myself or all my other colleagues, my doctors, we all read medicine and learned how to help the sick, the wounded and so on and so forth but we didn't have any war experience and we did not expect that because of that conflict between the, I don't know, Croats and Muslims, the Croats would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I'm very sorry but you're not answering my question. And it will be unnecessarily long. What I want to know is what made you indignant? What made you angry? Did the prisoners have any marks of having been beaten, tortured, or were they victims of some general diseases, contagious diseases where they were too cramped, too overcrowded in the cell? Will you explain that? Do not go into the past of that situation. Just give me the answer to what I've asked you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Right. When I personally entered the centre that I spoke about, I saw many people in one place. I did not see -- I did not see then anyone with some injuries. At that time, I did not see anyone like that. However, amongst those people, I saw some men who had, I don't know, some said, "Well, I'm taking medicines against high blood pressure, and here I don't have medicines or anything." For instance, then people, you understand what I'm driving at? That is individual men approached us, the doctors, and complained, saying, "Well, I don't have this medicine or that medicine. I need this or that." And so on. So that the fact that you have many people in one place, even if they are in good shape and healthy, will require some intervention. For instance, to make a step forward and then anticipate certain events, anticipate that perhaps an epidemic may break out or I don't know what, and that interventions maybe necessary because of this multitude of people in one place, because of all the requests that they told us about. I saw at that very moment that it was a very serious matter and that it needed to be addressed very seriously, and that in case of health care, one would have to urgently and systematically form a group to supervise and treat and so on. And that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you say after the attacks on the 9th of May, 1993, and other events that follow, that Bosnia remained intact and whole in one piece? That is at least what I gathered. Did you say that? Or perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean that Bosnia remained intact? What do you mean? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noted down, I wrote down what you were saying, what you said in this courtroom, that after the attacks of the 9th of May, and other events that ensued, that Bosnia remained intact and whole. Did I get you wrong or is it what you said? Perhaps you did not speak about that year, perhaps you were very fast. We have interpreters with us. Did you affirm that Bosnia remained intact and in one piece?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I spoke about that at all. I do not recall that in relation to the conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I do not insist. You spoke about Madam Minder and that she came to help, in view of the tragic situation in Konjic, and -- who is Mrs. Minder? Who is Madam Minder. And you said she needed authorisation to help you. Whose authorisation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember if it is Mrs. Minder or somebody like that. I need a document because I was reading documents, but I believe you're referring to a document that was sent to the International Red Cross, the International Red Cross, and she headed it at the time. She was responsible for it at the time. I think that is what it is about. And if that is so, and I think it is, then it is an international organisation which has no weapons, which has its staff unarmed and they cannot come to Konjic, cannot go to Croat villages where specifically a crime had been committed at the time because the Muslim forces, the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had blocked that area. She therefore needed their permission. Otherwise she could not do it. And that is what happened. We did not get the permit. We did not get the authorisation and we did nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Bagaric, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, I do on one question about arising from Judge Clark's questions about whether conditions in fact materially improved after the end of July, 1993. If I can have the usher's hopefully final assistance today by showing the witness P630.2? Which would be in the original binder, P630.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, because of the time, I'm not going to show you -- I don't have time to show you the other document but this is very, very similar to P638.1, which we looked at for sometime. This was a letter again from Mr. Bozic to Bruno Stojic. That 638.1 dated the 11th of October, 1993, and I submit, Mr. President, any one in the courtroom that compares the text they will find that the texts are virtually identical or extremely similar. Sir, do you see on this version of the document, 630.2 that notations from Mate Boban have been put on this document in which he writes to the chief of the military police, Mr. Valentin Choric, this is a very serious problem, please contact Mr. Bozic, sort the matter out within the limits of what is possible, and the requirements of humanitarian law. Put together rules and an organisation immediately. Report to me and describe the situation to date in the following manner, who, whom, where and when, 13 October, 1993, Boban." And also the notation, Mr. Boban's alleged hand, "Urgent, Boban."

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise. I don't know what you're talking about. I am being shown a document of the 10th of October, 1993. Is that the document? There is no number that you're talking about. What I have here is 01538326. Is that the document, that document was given me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's correct and you'll see -- excuse me, you will see on that document, sir, in the Croatian language, the hand written notations, in the upper right corner of the page.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. Go on. So what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that when these conditions in this report, which is the content of which is very similar to 638.1 from Mr. Bozic, found its way up to Mate Boban, Mate Boban's clear reaction was these matters had to be corrected immediately, and can we not understand from that that as of the 10th of October, 1993, they had not been corrected?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I have no idea about this document. I do not know who it is being sent to, why, I can read it and see. I had a look at it. It is repeated here, I don't know, large number of the wounded requiring hospital treatment, problem of medical supplies, setting up a clinic and so on and so forth, and I claim, I claim under full responsibility that this is therefore 10th October, 1993. As of the moment when I told you that we set up a medical team outside now what is called outside -- outside the centre, and the team which was set up in the centre, that in point of fact, it solved the major part of the problems. I'm sorry that you don't have it. I can't talk about a document which was written by somebody else, but I'm sorry that you do not have here a report. After all you did send me sometime ago the report of my doctors who say, therefore doctors who are saying, who are speaking something else than what is said here. Now, I do not know that this is a very serious problem. I do not know whether the centre has become a problem unto itself because they possibly do not know how to run it any more. They cannot handle all the problems of all sorts, that are indicated here. So I do not know that. But whether it comes to the medical care that I spoke about, and in the report of the doctor that I showed you sometime ago, it shows that it was definitely improved and that it was solved so I really cannot comment on this paper, I need time to have a look at it and so on. But I think that the generally has to do with the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. President, to the witness, sir, as a senior member of the Ministry of Defence, is it not true, and did you not know, that as a result of the international pressure brought to bear at the end of 1993, including about the conditions in the camps, Mate Boban was removed from office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question does not arise from the questions asked by Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree this question does not come out much Judge Clark's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I disagree because it goes to whether the conditions were in fact materially improved or not and when Mate Boban was removed as president partly because of this reason I think it goes directly to the question but I stand by the Court's rulings, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, my advice is that you withdraw this question at this moment since it's very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to withdraw the question, Your Honour. I think it's a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, if you'd like to answer, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not? The Prosecutor is entitled -- is right when he says that the centre has become a problem, meaning maintenance, meaning, I don't know, medical supplies, food supplies, and all sorts of problems that went with it. Yes, of course, it required additional effort and meant more work, just as any other unit and work related to that -- to it. I have no doubts about that. However, it is absolutely crazy to say after all the documents that I presented, I mean papers and testimonies of my doctors and a real situation there, that nothing changed there. When it comes to the medical care, I absolutely refuse any accusation in that regard, and I see absolutely no purpose in asking such questions, and that it should have been closed down? Well, would that it had never opened and not a single centre in Bosnia, ever. I agree about that. But I said that we prevented, we prevented, that is we allowed that people be extended health care. We prevented epidemics. We prevented suffering as much as we could. And that was a major progress. Whatever happened had those people suffered en masse or killed or fallen ill or -- I see no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no more time and that is what worries me. I wish to tell Your Honours that the cross-examination should have been interrupted at quarter to five, not five, it's two hours. I have two witnesses and my professor has not yet come, from now on, Your Honours, I will change the tactics of my direct examination, trying not to prejudice myself. These are either tactical moves to discuss it at such length or something else but I have to finish my witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you ever any question in your re-examination out of Judges questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question arising out of Her Honour Judge Diarra's questions which I think was unanswered. Judge Diarra asked rightfully and the doctor answered was the Heliodrom as a result of the conflict. It was your first question and later on it was what conditions when he found then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that the centre arose from the conflict, that it was the result of the conflict, but please very brief it's 7.00 can you please do it in one sentence? That arises from Her Honour Judge Diarra's question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia fought together in the Croat Defence Council and fought together against their common enemy, there was no -- detention of anyone by anyone. But the moment the Muslim units or rather members of the Muslim army left the Croat Defence Council and overnight, I don't know, took certain points, certain areas and when a conflict took place and when the mutual trust fell to the lowest possible point when nobody trusted anyone and when everybody doubted everything, that happened, and I think that is the principal cause of it. In order to prevent people from further taking up arms on behalf of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, doing mischief and so on and so forth so it arised from the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and finally can we have a look at 630.2 and 638.1? I do not have any questions but if you take those documents and I mean Your Honours, if you took these documents, I do not know what they look like in English because I do not know those English texts, but look at the Croatian originals. The Croatian texts are absolutely identical, the two texts are identical, absolutely, apart from the very last sentence, that is the last passage, all the eight items are absolutely identical. And now please look at the Croatian original. There is no signature and no stamp. How is that possible? Document 638.1, the Croatian original, no signature, no stamp, identical document with 630.2. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to help us. We appreciate it very much. All of us wish you good luck in your future. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even shake hands with the accused and yet they are here all the time, those people who are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You are not allowed to shake hands with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's five minutes past the time. We have no time for the admission of the documents. I wish both parties will submit their written submissions in one week's time, including their objections to the other party's documents. We will resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
